title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the hermes-consultant-advanced series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, a high-potential operator two years from principal is already performing well. Which relationship do they actually need?
options: Mentorship on judgment and sponsorship into the room where the client relationship and the P and L live, because delivering more management is how a firm loses its best people.
More management, because objectives, utilization, and role performance are still unproven.
Coaching on how to work faster within the current role before any new exposure.
All four relationships at once so nothing is missed.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the advanced discipline is triage, and management answers whether someone is doing the job while sponsorship creates the opportunity mentorship turns into capability.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, the lesson says a conversation where the principal explains how they would have handled a situation does not transfer judgment. What does?
options: Handing the operator the written standard and letting them read it until it is memorized.
Letting the operator shadow the principal for a full year before making any decision.
Reviewing the operator's output against the acceptance criteria after each delivery.
A progression of observation, then simulated decisions where the operator commits before the principal reveals their answer, then earned autonomy with a backstop, then judgment with no backstop.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the delta between the operator's committed judgment and the principal's is the actual pedagogical content, and the discipline is to answer with the question rather than the answer.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Mentorship and Developing Senior Delivery Talent”, what distinguishes senior delivery talent from a mid-level operator?
options: More years of experience across a wider range of clients.
A higher utilization rate on client-billable work.
The ability to author the standard rather than only meet it: write the acceptance criteria, place the gate, review someone else's work, and own the estimate and the client relationship.
The habit of escalating fewer problems to the principal over time.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the step up is the move from executing within a framework to owning it, and that nobody becomes ready by being told they are not ready.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, what is the real unit of scaling?
options: The distance between the principal and any work product that crosses the client threshold, measured by how many current products would degrade if the principal vanished tomorrow.
Annual revenue growth, since that is what funds the next hire.
Headcount, because a larger team can carry more concurrent engagements.
The number of signed engagements per quarter.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice with twelve employees is usually still a solo practice with twelve employees if every deliverable still passes through one head to be trusted.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, why must the three separations happen in order?
options: Because the review gate cannot be built until there is a second seller to fund it.
Because the offer cannot be detached from the founder until the standard is certified.
Because a firm that builds a second seller before a second reviewer can sell more work than it can safely deliver, and the extra revenue funds a quality collapse.
Because capacity cannot be separated from the calendar until the founder stops billing.
questions.explanation: The lesson says each separation depends on the one before it, and separations built out of order fail.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Case Study: Scaling a Practice from Solo to Team”, a principal can spend the next quarter personally running one more flagship engagement, or building a third lead and packaging a new service line. How should the options be compared?
options: On revenue, because the flagship engagement funds the development later.
On the principal's own utilization, because that is the scarce resource.
On client satisfaction, because the flagship account is the firm's reputation.
On distance moved: which option increases the work the system can carry without the principal in the path, even though the busy option wins on revenue.
questions.explanation: The lesson says revenue grows under the busy option while the distance metric does not move, which is how a firm grows revenue while remaining a solo practice.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, why should a practice model at the unit level instead of in annual revenue and profit?
options: Because yearly totals hide the fixed costs that unit modeling exposes.
Because the unit is where the levers live, a single price, a single delivery cost, a single sales volume, which is what lets the model answer what-if questions.
Because unit economics are required by lenders before a practice can raise cash.
Because annual profit is too volatile to be modeled at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson says you cannot act directly on annual profit, but you can act on one unit's price, cost, or volume, which is what the model is built to test.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, Delta Forge shows healthy per-unit contribution and a practice margin of about 142,000 a year, but a stress-case runway of only about 4.8 months. What is the founder's correct first job?
options: Build a fourth rung of the ladder, since the healthy margin proves the firm can afford it.
Raise the price of the flagship build so the buffer grows faster.
Cut the fixed base below the six-month line by letting a lead go.
Bank a larger cash buffer and book retained, recurring units that lower net burn, because below the runway floor the compounding choice is not affordable.
questions.explanation: The lesson concludes that margin is the fuel and runway is the tank, so the founder must refill the tank before spending the fuel on a non-delivery bet.

questions.question: Per the lesson “The Financial Model: Units, Margins, and Runway”, what distinction does the lesson draw between modeling and forecasting?
options: Keep the model rigorous, the prices, costs, contributions, fixed base, and runway formula, and keep the forecast humble, since the forecast is always wrong in the details.
Model monthly and forecast annually, because yearly forecasts are more accurate.
Model the units and forecast the runway, because runway cannot be modeled.
Model conservatively and forecast optimistically so the firm is not under-investing.
questions.explanation: The lesson says to spend attention on the structure you control rather than pretending the revenue forecast is precise.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, what is the tell of a real partnership rather than a vendor relationship?
options: The client renews the contract without negotiating the terms each time.
The client reports high satisfaction in an annual review.
Access: the client brings the practice problems before they are urgent and consults it on what is not yet contracted.
The client pays a recurring fee rather than paying per project.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a satisfied client can still leave and a serial one-off buyer renews out of convenience; access is the raw material that can only be earned, never sold.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, what is the danger the lesson names for a retainer that is a block of hours the client can burn on whatever they choose?
options: It exposes the practice to unlimited scope risk with no ceiling.
It degrades into a subscription for the client's own time management, which is selling time with extra steps and none of the transparency of time-and-materials.
It makes the recurring revenue unpredictable for both sides.
It prevents the practice from charging a value-based premium later.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a durable retainer is tied to outcomes or a delivery cadence the client can feel, not to a pool of hours.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Long-Term Client Partnerships and Recurring Revenue”, when is a retained client genuinely an asset rather than a comfortable drain?
options: When its recurring revenue grows every quarter without added delivery cost.
When its gross margin exceeds the practice's blended delivery margin.
When its retention rate is above the practice's historical average.
When the stream of value it produces over its lifetime beats the best alternative use of the delivery capability it holds.
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the portfolio lens inside a single account and says the principal must measure rather than assume, because comfort is the most dangerous thing a drain has going for it.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, what test does the capstone give for telling a go-to-market plan from an aspiration?
options: Whether the plan has been approved by an advisor outside the practice.
Whether every section names a target revenue number and a date to hit it.
Whether you can hand the document to a competent person who knows nothing about the practice and have them run it for a quarter.
Whether the plan includes both inbound and outbound motions in equal measure.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a plan is executable by someone other than its author; if a section reads as a resolution rather than a decision, it is an aspiration.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, why is delivery excellence not enough on its own?
options: Because the market cannot evaluate delivery until the practice is already in the room, so the buyer buys the promise as represented in positioning, offer, and proof.
Because excellent delivery always leads to complacency about quality.
Because referrals dry up once a practice stops billing hourly.
Because enterprise buyers evaluate delivery before they will agree to a discovery call.
questions.explanation: The lesson says weak go-to-market fails because the work is invisible to the people who need it, not because the work is bad.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Capstone, Build a Complete Go-to-Market Plan for Your Own Practice”, the plan says every part of a go-to-market plan is a decision. What does deciding mean there?
options: Choosing the marketing automation the practice will run the plan on.
A commitment that closes off alternatives, such as naming a segment deciding whom you will deliberately not pursue.
Setting a quarterly revenue target that the team is accountable to.
Selecting which competitor the practice will position against.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a section that does not close off an alternative is an aspiration and will not survive a quarter of real operations.
